A release has two steps: upload every new asset under a versioned name, then switch the manifest to point at those names.

The upload comes first because the manifest is what browsers follow. Once it changes, any browser that loads it will immediately request the files it names. If those files weren't already uploaded, the browser would get 404s and render a broken page. Uploading first means every name in the new manifest already resolves when the switch happens. Versioned names make this safe, because the uploads don't overwrite anything the current manifest uses. Until the switch, the live site doesn't see them.

We keep the old assets because some browsers fetched the previous manifest before the switch and are still running it. Those pages will keep requesting the old names, for example when lazy-loading a script, a stylesheet or an image. If we deleted the old files, those sessions would break partway through. Keeping them means both the old manifest and the new one fully resolve, so every browser gets a consistent set of files no matter when it loaded the page.

Each release has two steps. First, we upload every new asset under a versioned name. Then we switch the manifest to point at those names.

The upload comes first so the manifest never references a file that isn't there yet. If we switched the manifest first, any browser that loaded it before the upload finished would request missing assets and get a broken page. Because the files are already in place, the switch takes effect for everyone at once.

We keep the old assets because some browsers already loaded the previous manifest and will keep requesting the files it lists. Versioned names let the old and new files exist side by side. If we deleted the old ones, those browsers would get errors in the middle of a session.

A release happens in two steps: first we upload every new asset under a versioned name (for example, `app.3f9c2.js`), then we switch the manifest so it points to those new names.

The upload comes first because the manifest is what browsers follow. If we switched it before the files existed, any browser that fetched the new manifest in that gap would request assets that aren't there yet, and the page would break. Uploading first means every name the new manifest mentions is already live when the manifest changes, so the switch itself is the only moment the release takes effect.

We keep the old assets because switching the manifest doesn't update browsers that already loaded the previous one. Those pages still request the old versioned names, for example when lazy-loading a chunk. If we deleted the old files, those sessions would hit missing assets mid-use. Because names are versioned, old and new files never collide, so both releases can be served side by side.

When we release, we first upload every new asset (JS, CSS, images) under a versioned name, such as `app.4f2c1a.js`, and only then switch the manifest so it points at those new names.

The upload comes first because the manifest switch is the moment the release goes live. As soon as the manifest names `app.4f2c1a.js`, browsers start requesting it. If that file isn't already uploaded, those requests fail and users get a broken page. Uploading first means every name the new manifest references already exists when anyone reads it.

We keep the old assets because the switch doesn't reach everyone at once. A browser that loaded the previous manifest a minute before the release still holds its old references and will keep requesting files like `app.91be07.js` as it lazy-loads chunks or navigates. If we deleted those files at the switch, that user's page would break mid-session. Because versioned names never collide, the old and new sets can sit side by side, so both the previous release and the current one keep working.
